nameStory: The name "spikerush" comes from the plant's spiky flower clusters that sit atop thin, rush-like stems. The "matted" part refers to how this species forms dense, low-growing carpets or mats along wet shorelines and mudflats. Unlike many of its taller spikerush cousins, this one stays close to the ground and spreads horizontally.
description: Matted Spikerush is a small, grass-like wetland plant that forms dense, low mats along muddy shores and shallow water edges. It grows only 2-6 inches tall, with thin, bright green stems topped by tiny brown flower spikes. Instead of growing upright like most spikerushes, it creeps along the ground on underground runners, creating carpets of vegetation. This humble little sedge belongs to the sedge family, not the grass family, despite its grass-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, low mats that spread horizontally rather than growing tall - the stems lie nearly flat against wet mud or sand and feel springy underfoot

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, bright green stems only 2-6 inches long that feel firm and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny brown or tan flower spikes at stem tips, about the size of a grain of rice, with a papery texture when touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: No true leaves - just small brown sheaths that wrap around the base of each stem like tiny paper collars

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in wet, muddy areas that are often underwater in spring but may dry out partially in summer

habitat: Look for Matted Spikerush along the muddy edges of ponds, lakes, and slow streams throughout New England, especially where water levels fluctuate seasonally. It thrives in the wet, sandy or muddy soils of shorelines, often growing right at the waterline where it can be partially submerged. You'll commonly find it mixed with other wetland plants like arrowhead and pickerelweed.

seasonality.spring: New bright green shoots emerge from underground runners as water levels are typically highest. The plant forms its characteristic low mats as stems begin spreading horizontally.
seasonality.summer: Tiny brown flower spikes appear at stem tips, and the dense green mats are most visible as water levels often drop, exposing more muddy shoreline.
seasonality.fall: Stems begin to yellow and die back, though the underground runner system remains alive. Seeds disperse from the dried brown flower heads.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only the underground runners to survive freezing temperatures and ice.

funFact: Despite being one of the smallest spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is actually a champion at preventing soil erosion - its dense network of underground runners can hold muddy shorelines together so effectively that it's sometimes used in wetland restoration projects to stabilize banks.
confusionNotes: Most other spikerushes grow upright and tall, making Matted Spikerush's low, creeping habit quite distinctive. If you see a spikerush forming a carpet instead of standing up like tiny green soldiers, you've likely found this species. Remember: "Matted means flat" - it's the only spikerush that hugs the ground.
contextualKnowledge: Like all sedges, spikerushes have a helpful identifying rhyme: "Sedges have edges" - their stems are triangular or have ridges, unlike the round, hollow stems of true grasses. The sedge family is often overlooked by casual nature observers, but these plants are ecological powerhouses in wetland ecosystems.
compareHints: Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright. Needle Spikerush is similarly small but grows in tiny upright tufts, while Common Spikerush towers over this species at 1-4 feet tall. If you're looking at a spikerush that's forming a carpet rather than standing up straight, you've found the matted variety.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
